Level weirs that are out of tolerance using the adjustment points

Inspect weir levelness and baffle condition on each clarifier

Hold loading when the volatile acid to alkalinity ratio begins to rise
Set the sustainable loading rate as the operating target
Measure feed sludge flow and volatile solids over a representative week

tasks.explanation: Loading is calculated from measured feed before it is increased, stability indicators guard each step, and the sustainable rate becomes the target.

Transfer seed from a healthy digester if available
Resume feeding at a low rate only after acids begin to fall
Check temperature and mixing for a process cause
Confirm the trend with volatile acids, alkalinity, and pH testing

tasks.explanation: Testing confirms souring before feed is cut, buffering and seeding support recovery, and refeeding waits for acids to fall.

Reassess gas production and solids profile after mixing is restored

Estimate active volume from temperature and solids profiles
Check mixer or gas recirculation equipment run times and condition

tasks.explanation: Profiles reveal dead zones before equipment is blamed, deficient mixing is repaired, and gas response confirms the evaluation.

Verify temperature readings with a second instrument

Hold temperature changes to about one degree Celsius per day
Log the stable temperature and the heating settings that hold it

Calculate current volatile solids reduction from feed and digested sludge data
Check detention time at current feed rates and digester volume in service
Confirm temperature and mixing are at target conditions

Isolate and lock out the gas equipment to be worked on
Issue the work permit with gas test results recorded
Test the atmosphere for methane, hydrogen sulfide, and oxygen
Purge or vent the isolated section following the site procedure

Set feed pump schedules to deliver the target blend through the day
Check thickener operation for each stream separately

Record the settings that give the best capture and cake solids together
Balance throughput against cake dryness at the chosen settings
Measure feed solids, cake solids, and centrate solids at current settings

Collect a representative sludge sample and record its solids and pH
Select the polymer on performance per tonne of dry solids and order accordingly
Compare cake solids, capture, and throughput for each trial
Trial the best two polymers on the press at matched doses
Bench test each polymer at several doses using a consistent drainage test

tasks.prompt: Mixed liquor settles poorly and the secondary clarifier blanket is rising despite normal flows and normal wasting.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: SVI rose from 95 to 240 mL/g over ten days while MLSS held near 2400 mg/L.
Microscopy shows abundant filamentous organisms bridging between floc particles, with floc structure otherwise intact.
A bench settling test leaves a cloudy supernatant above a bulky, slow settling sludge.
Effluent BOD remains low at 8 mg/L, showing carbon removal is still working.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Filamentous bulking is causing poor compaction and blanket rise while treatment itself remains intact
The sludge is too old and needs a large increase in wasting to restore settling
A toxic load has killed the biomass and settling has failed from deflocculation
Hydraulic overload is washing solids over the clarifier weirs

inference.explanation: Only filamentous bulking fits all points. Microscopy shows filaments bridging floc, SVI is very high at normal MLSS, and the bench test shows bulky settling with cloudy supernatant. Low effluent BOD contradicts biomass death, blanket rise at normal flow contradicts hydraulic washout, and old sludge alone does not explain the filament bridges seen.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Diluted SVI and microscopy filament abundance log for the past two weeks
Effluent flow total for the month
Primary clarifier blanket log

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: The log shows filament abundance rising with SVI over the same ten days, matching the blanket rise.
clueText.nc-b: Monthly flow totals cannot test filament growth.
clueText.nc-c: The primary blanket log covers a different unit and does not test mixed liquor settling.

evidence.label: Microscopy of the foam shows dense Nocardia type filaments concentrated in the foam compared with the mixed liquor.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Detergent in the influent is creating a white surfactant foam across the plant
Low dissolved oxygen is causing a young sludge foam from rapid growth
A grease spill is floating as a one time surface layer
Long SRT Nocardia foaming is building a stable foam blanket on the older train

inference.explanation: Surfactant foam would be white, fragile, and plant wide, not brown, stable, and limited to one train. Low DO young sludge foam does not concentrate Nocardia filaments. The paired train comparison, the microscopy, and the stability on spraying all point to Nocardia foaming at long SRT.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Influent detergent survey for the service area
Blower airflow log for the week
Foam microscopy and SRT record comparison between the two parallel trains

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: A detergent survey cannot explain foam limited to one train with filament rich microscopy.
clueText.nc-b: Airflow logs do not test filament type in the foam.
clueText.nc-c: Foam samples stay filament rich and the older train SRT is more than double the younger train, matching the foam pattern.

evidence.label: MLSS fell from 2600 to 1400 mg/L in four days after the wasting increase.

inference.explanation: Filaments are now few, which contradicts filamentous bulking as the current cause. No drive failure is recorded and influent strength is not shown to change. The timing, the MLSS drop, the F/M rise, and the weak young floc on microscopy all follow the wasting increase.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

clueText.nc-b: The trend shows settling worsening only after wasting rose and MLSS fell, with F/M climbing in step.
clueText.nc-c: Drive current does not test biomass inventory.

tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: Solids retention time calculates at 28 days, well above the plant target band of 8 to 12 days.
Microscopy shows very small, dense floc with almost no filaments and many dispersed fine particles.
SVI is low at 62 mL/g and the sludge settles fast, leaving a turbid supernatant in the bench test.
Oxygen uptake is low and the mixed liquor looks dark and old on inspection.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Excess aeration is shearing large healthy floc into fines
An overaged sludge at excessive SRT is breaking into pin floc that settles fast but leaves a turbid supernatant
Filamentous bulking is preventing the sludge from settling
Low SRT washout is carrying young biomass over the weir

inference.explanation: Low SVI with fast settling contradicts filamentous bulking, which gives slow bulky settling. Washout from low SRT is contradicted by the calculated 28 day SRT. The old dark liquor, low uptake, and small dense floc at very long SRT support pin floc from overaged sludge.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: SRT calculation record and bench settling supernatant clarity log
Blower discharge pressure log
Return sludge pump run log

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-b: Blower pressure does not measure sludge age.
clueText.nc-c: Return pump run times do not test floc age or size.

evidence.label: Clarifier influent nitrate is 18 mg/L as N and dissolved oxygen entering the clarifier is low at 0.4 mg/L.
A bench sample of settled sludge releases nitrogen gas bubbles and floats within two hours at room temperature.

Filamentous bulking is preventing the sludge from settling in the first place
Septic primary sludge is gassing and rising in the secondary clarifier
Excess return rate is hydraulically lifting the blanket

inference.explanation: Bulking sludge settles poorly from the start, but this sludge settles and then rises hours later with gas. No septic primary link is shown, and the return rate is normal. High nitrate, low DO, complete nitrification, and gas release in the bench sample support denitrification in the blanket.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Primary sludge volatile acids log
Headworks screenings log
Clarifier feed nitrate and DO record with blanket rising observations by hour

clueText.nc-b: Screenings records do not explain clarifier rising sludge.
clueText.nc-c: The record shows rising clumps only when feed nitrate is high and DO is low, matching denitrification timing.

tasks.prompt: After a blower outage, the plant returns to service but settling stays poor for a week with dark, odorous mixed liquor.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: The outage left the basin without air for 14 hours and DO read zero through the night.
Mixed liquor turned dark and septic, and microscopy shows many dead filaments and broken floc a day later.
Effluent BOD rose during the outage and is recovering slowly as fresh growth returns.
A reseeded bench reactor fed the same sewage settled normally within three days.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A filamentous bulking organism has permanently taken over the plant
The clarifier has a mechanical failure that began during the outage
Influent toxicity entered during the outage and persists in the feed
Prolonged zero DO during the outage killed and lysed biomass, leaving damaged floc that must regrow

inference.explanation: Bulking takeover does not explain dead filaments and broken floc right after zero DO. No clarifier mechanical fault is recorded. The reseeded bench reactor settling on the same feed argues against a persistent feed toxin and supports biomass damage from the outage.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Blower outage timeline with microscopy and effluent BOD recovery record
Influent metals survey
Clarifier drive inspection sheet

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: The timeline ties the damage markers to the 14 hour zero DO period, with recovery tracking new growth.
clueText.nc-b: A metals survey cannot test outage related biomass damage.
clueText.nc-c: Drive inspection covers mechanics, not floc condition after an outage.

tasks.prompt: Chemical phosphorus removal is inconsistent from day to day at a constant dose and constant influent load.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: Alum day tank concentration varies because the dilution water valve leaks variably into the tank.
Tank strength tests range from 28 percent to 48 percent against a 48 percent nominal product.
Dosing pump delivers constant volume, so chemical mass varies with tank strength.
A trial isolating the leaking valve held tank strength steady and effluent phosphorus stabilized.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Operators change the dose without logging it
Variable day tank dilution from the leaking valve is varying the true alum mass dose
Influent phosphorus load varies more than the records show
The phosphorus analyzer drifts randomly each day

inference.explanation: Load records and analyzer duplicates are steady, and pump logs show no unlogged dose changes. Tank strength measurements varying with the leak and stabilizing after isolation support dilution as the cause.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Day tank strength test series with valve isolation trial record
Phosphorus analyzer duplicate sheet
Dosing pump log

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: Tank strength held at nominal after isolation, and effluent phosphorus steadied at the same pump setting.
clueText.nc-b: Duplicates confirm analyzer stability.
clueText.nc-c: Pump logs show constant settings throughout.

tasks.prompt: Two identical aeration trains settle very differently, and only the poorly settling train receives recycle from the dewatering unit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: Train A SVI is 110 mL/g and Train B SVI is 235 mL/g at the same MLSS and loading.
Dewatering centrate, high in ammonia and fine solids, returns only to the head of Train B.
Microscopy shows filaments abundant in Train B and scarce in Train A.
Swapping the centrate return to Train A on trial moved the settling problem with it over two weeks.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Train B clarifier is smaller and overloads before Train A
A toxic discharge enters Train B through a separate sewer
The centrate recycle load to Train B is driving its filamentous bulking, as shown by the swap trial
Train B has a faulty aeration grid that Train A does not have

inference.explanation: The swap trial moving the problem with the centrate is the decisive check and rules out fixed train faults such as grids or clarifier size. No separate toxic sewer is recorded. Filament growth tracking the recycle stream supports the centrate explanation.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Blower nameplate data sheet
Influent flow split record
Centrate return routing log and SVI trend for both trains across the swap trial

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: Nameplate data cannot test a recycle stream effect.
clueText.nc-b: Flow split records show equal flows and do not explain the crossover.
clueText.nc-c: The SVI trend crossed over after the swap, with Train A rising and Train B recovering at unchanged total load.

tasks.prompt: Sludge age keeps climbing even though the wasting rate was increased twice this month.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: WAS concentration fell from 8000 to 3800 mg/L as the blanket thinned, so mass wasted barely changed.
MLSS inventory stayed near 2500 mg/L because effluent solids losses also rose.
A mass balance check shows wasted mass per day nearly flat despite higher WAS flow.
Clarifier effluent TSS rose from 12 to 34 mg/L over the same period.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The laboratory is overreading MLSS and the age is actually falling
Higher WAS flow at much lower WAS concentration is wasting little extra mass, so sludge age stays high
The wasting pumps are broken and move no sludge at all
Influent solids have doubled and are replacing the wasted mass

inference.explanation: Pumps are moving more flow, not zero, so a total pump failure is contradicted. Influent solids are not shown to double. The mass balance using the falling WAS concentration explains flat wasted mass and rising age without lab error.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Effluent ammonia log
WAS flow and concentration mass balance sheet for the month
Influent flow total for the year

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: Ammonia results do not measure solids inventory.
clueText.nc-b: The sheet shows wasted kilograms per day nearly unchanged while WAS litres per day doubled.
clueText.nc-c: Annual flow totals cannot test a wasting mass balance.

tasks.prompt: A sudden foam and bulking upset follows a large drop in mixed liquor temperature after a cold snap.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: Basin temperature fell from 16 C to 8 C in five days and stayed low for two weeks.
Microscopy shows Microthrix type filaments increasing steadily through the cold period.
SVI climbed from 120 to 210 mL/g while DO and loading stayed in their normal bands.
A bench reactor warmed to 15 C on the same feed settled better than its twin held at 8 C.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Cold temperature selection for Microthrix filaments is driving the bulking during the cold snap
A grease discharge during the cold snap is coating the floc
Nitrifier washout has removed the bacteria that hold floc together
Low DO from blower icing is the primary cause of the filaments

inference.explanation: DO stayed in its normal band, which argues against a low DO cause. No grease discharge is recorded, and nitrifiers are not the floc structure at issue. The warming bench comparison and the Microthrix increase support cold selection.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Temperature trend with paired bench reactor settling record at two temperatures
Blower intake inspection log
Influent grease survey

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: The warmed reactor held a lower SVI on the same feed while the cold twin bulked, matching the plant trend.
clueText.nc-b: Intake inspection does not test temperature selection in the basin.
clueText.nc-c: A grease survey cannot explain the paired temperature result.

tasks.prompt: Effluent quality is excellent but the plant cannot keep MLSS up, and the sludge looks young and dispersed.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: Solids retention time calculates at 2.1 days against a design target of 6 to 8 days.
F/M ratio is high at 0.65 per day and oxygen demand spikes after each feed peak.
Microscopy shows small floc, many free swimming bacteria, and active stalked ciliates scarce.
Raising SRT on a pilot lane to 7 days produced larger floc and stable MLSS on the same feed.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Filamentous bulking is washing the MLSS out over the weirs
A toxic influent is killing biomass as fast as it grows
The clarifier is leaking solids through a broken baffle
Excessive wasting keeps SRT too short for a stable mature biomass inventory

inference.explanation: Microscopy shows scarce filaments, not bulking washout, and no baffle fault is recorded. A persistent toxin would not be corrected by longer SRT in the pilot lane. Short SRT, high F/M, and young microscopy support overwasting.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Clarifier baffle inspection sheet
Influent toxicity screening log
SRT and F/M calculation record with pilot lane comparison

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: Baffle inspection covers a mechanical fault not seen in the microscopy.
clueText.nc-b: Toxicity screening does not explain the SRT response in the pilot.
clueText.nc-c: The pilot lane at 7 days SRT built stable MLSS and larger floc while the plant lane at 2.1 days stayed dispersed.

tasks.prompt: Bulking returns every winter at the same plant while summer settling is consistently good.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: SVI exceeds 200 mL/g each January to March and returns below 120 mL/g each summer.
Microscopy each winter shows the same cold favouring filament type dominant.
Fats, oils, and grease loads from the collection system rise in winter as grease releases in slugs.
A heated pilot reactor on winter sewage settles well while an unheated twin bulks.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Higher winter flows alone wash solids out each year
A winter industrial discharge is toxic to floc formers every year
Seasonal cold and grease slug conditions together select for the winter filament population
The winter operator crew operates the plant differently and causes the bulking

inference.explanation: Crew changes do not explain the heated pilot result on the same sewage. Winter flows are not shown above capacity. The repeated microscopy, the grease slug pattern, and the heated twin settling well support seasonal selection.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Annual flow summary
Seasonal SVI and microscopy archive with paired heated pilot record
Staff schedule archive

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: Annual flows hide the seasonal pattern that matters here.
clueText.nc-b: The archive shows the same filament dominant each winter, and the heated pilot settled while the cold twin bulked on identical feed.
clueText.nc-c: Staff schedules cannot test temperature selection.

tasks.prompt: Effluent ammonia rose from 1 to 14 mg/L over a week while effluent BOD stayed low and stable.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: Aeration basin temperature fell from 15 C to 9 C after a cold influent change.
Solids retention time calculates at 5 days, near the minimum for nitrifiers at this temperature.
Alkalinity in the effluent fell and basin pH drifted from 7.2 to 6.6.
A bench reactor held at 12 days SRT nitrified fully on the same sewage at the same temperature.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Excess wasting yesterday removed the entire nitrifier population at once
Cold temperature with marginal SRT is washing out slow growing nitrifiers faster than they can regrow
A toxic discharge has killed all bacteria including the carbon removers
Low DO alone explains the loss because carbon removal also failed

inference.explanation: Carbon removal stayed good, which contradicts a general toxic kill or a DO failure severe enough to stop all biology. A single day of wasting does not explain a week long trend. The bench reactor at longer SRT nitrifying at the same temperature supports SRT washout of nitrifiers.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: SRT calculation and bench reactor nitrification record at matched temperature
Influent metals results
Chlorine residual log

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: The bench unit at 12 days SRT held effluent ammonia below 2 mg/L while the plant at 5 days climbed, at the same feed and temperature.
clueText.nc-b: Metals results do not test sludge age for nitrifiers.
clueText.nc-c: Chlorine records cover disinfection, not nitrification.

tasks.prompt: Nitrification is lost each afternoon but recovers overnight, and ammonia peaks match the daily load peak.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: Basin DO falls to 0.6 mg/L at peak load and returns to 2.4 mg/L overnight.
Oxygen uptake rate tests show demand at peak exceeds the blower capacity at its current setting.
Ammonia breakthrough occurs only during the low DO afternoon window.
A trial raising afternoon airflow held DO above 1.8 mg/L and ammonia stayed low that day.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Oxygen supply at peak load is insufficient for nitrifiers, so nitrification stalls each afternoon
Nitrifiers have washed out completely and cannot recover overnight
Alkalinity is exhausted all day and pH blocks nitrification continuously
A daily toxic slug arrives each afternoon and kills nitrifiers

inference.explanation: Washout cannot recover overnight, and a continuous alkalinity block would not follow the DO window. No toxic slug is recorded. The airflow trial holding ammonia low at the same load directly supports peak oxygen limitation.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Effluent pH monthly summary
Wasting log for the month
Continuous DO trend with the afternoon airflow trial record

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: Monthly pH summaries hide the daily DO window.
clueText.nc-b: Wasting logs do not test peak oxygen supply.
clueText.nc-c: The trial day shows ammonia flat through the peak once DO was held above 1.8 mg/L.

tasks.prompt: Effluent ammonia and nitrite both rise together while nitrate falls, a pattern the operators call partial nitrification.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: Effluent nitrite rose from 0.2 to 4.5 mg/L as N while ammonia rose to 9 mg/L.
Basin DO has been held low at 0.8 mg/L to save energy for two weeks.
Alkalinity and pH remain adequate at 180 mg/L and 7.1.
A bench test at DO 2.0 mg/L converted ammonia fully to nitrate with little nitrite on the same liquor.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Low alkalinity is stopping both nitrification steps equally
High ammonia load has exceeded the design capacity of the basin
Free ammonia toxicity from high pH is inhibiting the nitrite oxidizers
Low DO is limiting the nitrite oxidizers more than the ammonia oxidizers, so nitrite accumulates

inference.explanation: Alkalinity and pH are adequate and pH is neutral, which contradicts alkalinity exhaustion and high pH free ammonia inhibition. Load is not shown above design. The bench recovery at higher DO supports DO limitation of the second step.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Influent ammonia load summary
DO setpoint history with bench nitrification test at two DO levels
Alkalinity delivery log

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: Load summaries do not explain nitrite specific accumulation.
clueText.nc-b: The bench liquor at 2.0 mg/L DO cleared nitrite while the plant liquor at 0.8 mg/L accumulated it.
clueText.nc-c: Alkalinity deliveries do not test DO limitation.

tasks.prompt: A plant loses nitrification within days of switching its basin to a new chemical cleaning agent used on site.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional Ontario wastewater plant case. Readings are from the stated period unless a bench, pilot, or paired unit check is noted. Archived plant records are available for follow up.

evidence.label: The new cleaner contains a quaternary ammonium disinfectant and wash water drains to the aeration basin.
Carbon BOD removal dipped only slightly while ammonia removal collapsed.
Oxygen uptake by nitrifiers in a bench test fell 80 percent when cleaner wash water was added.
The same bench test showed carbon uptake fell only 10 percent with the same addition.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Overwasting that week removed the nitrifier inventory
Low alkalinity developed the same week and stopped nitrification
The disinfectant cleaner reaching the basin is selectively inhibiting the sensitive nitrifiers
Cold weather arriving the same week washed out the nitrifiers

inference.explanation: The selective bench result, with nitrifier uptake falling far more than carbon uptake, points to inhibition rather than washout or alkalinity, neither of which is shown to change. Timing with the cleaner switch supports the disinfectant route.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best distinguishes the supported explanation from the alternatives?

options.label: Cleaner product record and bench oxygen uptake inhibition test results
Temperature trend for the week
Wasting log for the week

nextClue.explanation: This check tests the supported explanation directly against the alternatives. The other choices do not isolate the cause shown by the evidence.

clueText.nc-a: Bench nitrifier uptake fell sharply with cleaner addition while carbon uptake held, matching the plant pattern.
clueText.nc-b: Temperature alone does not explain selective nitrifier inhibition in the bench test.
clueText.nc-c: Wasting logs do not test chemical inhibition.
